title: The Development of Music Technology
claim: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) was famously recorded on 4-track
source: Wikipedia — Sgt Pepper's article confirms 4-track recording on EMI Studer J37 machines
notes: Correct. The album was indeed recorded on four-track equipment.

title: The Development of Music Technology
claim: MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) was introduced in 1983
source: Wikipedia — MIDI article: 'The MIDI specification was published in August 1983'
notes: Correct.

title: The Development of Music Technology
claim: Roland TR-808 — Early drum machines used analogue synthesis
source: Wikipedia — TR-808 article confirms 'generates sounds using analog synthesis rather than by playing samples'
notes: Correct. TR-808 used analog subtractive synthesis.

title: The Development of Music Technology
claim: The Mellotron was an early analogue tape-based sampler — it played pre-recorded tape strips of real instruments when keys were pressed
source: Wikipedia — Mellotron article: 'uses the same concept as a sampler, but generates its sound using analogue recordings on audio tape'
notes: Correct.

title: The Development of Music Technology
claim: ADAT (Alesis Digital Audio Tape) made digital multitrack recording affordable for home studios by recording 8 tracks onto VHS tape
source: Wikipedia — ADAT article: 'eight digital audio tracks onto the same S-VHS tape used by consumer VCRs'
notes: ADAT used S-VHS tape, not standard VHS. S-VHS uses the same cassette shell but is technically a higher-quality format. The lesson simplifies to 'VHS tape'. Acceptable at GCSE level but technically imprecise.

title: Food Safety: Bacteria, Allergens & Intolerances
claim: Campylobacter — the most common cause of food poisoning in the UK
source: NHS — food poisoning page confirms campylobacter as 'the most common cause of food poisoning in the UK'
notes: Correct.

title: Food Safety: Bacteria, Allergens & Intolerances
claim: Listeria — unusual because it can grow at refrigerator temperatures. Particularly dangerous for pregnant women, as it can cause miscarriage
source: Wikipedia — Listeria article confirms growth at 4°C and danger during pregnancy
notes: Correct. Listeria can grow at refrigerator temperatures and causes listeriosis which can lead to miscarriage.

title: Food Safety: Bacteria, Allergens & Intolerances
claim: Bacillus cereus — produces toxins when cooked food is left at room temperature too long. Reheating does not destroy the toxin
source: Wikipedia — B. cereus article: cereulide toxin 'can withstand 121°C for 90 minutes'
notes: Correct. The emetic toxin (cereulide) is heat-resistant.

title: Food Safety: Bacteria, Allergens & Intolerances
claim: Staphylococcus aureus — carried on human skin, especially in the nose and throat. The toxin it produces is heat-resistant, so reheating does not make the food safe
source: Wikipedia — S. aureus article confirms nasal/throat carriage; food safety literature confirms enterotoxin heat stability
notes: Nasal/skin carriage confirmed. S. aureus enterotoxins are widely established in food microbiology as heat-stable (survive boiling). Claim is correct.

title: Food Safety: Bacteria, Allergens & Intolerances
claim: UK food law requires all food businesses to declare the presence of 14 specific allergens. Sulphur dioxide and sulphites (above 10mg/kg)
source: FSA allergen guidance: 14 allergens confirmed; sulphites threshold '> 10 parts per million' = 10 mg/kg (mass fraction equivalence)
notes: 10 mg/kg and 10 ppm are equivalent for food mass fractions. The threshold and list are correct.

title: Food Commodities & Their Place in the Diet
claim: Long-life (UHT) milk is produced by heating to 135°C for 2–4 seconds, destroying all bacteria
source: Wikipedia Pasteurization article: UHT is '135°C for 1–2 seconds'. Wikipedia UHT Processing article: 'above 140°C for 2–5 seconds'. EU/UK food regulations cite 135°C.
notes: The temperature (135°C) is supported by the Pasteurization article and EU regulations. The duration (2-4 seconds) is slightly wider than the 1-2 seconds standard; the upper bound of 4 seconds is not supported. This is a minor imprecision rather than a fabrication — the core claim is essentially correct.

title: Food Commodities & Their Place in the Diet
claim: Potatoes should be stored in a cool, dark, dry location to prevent greening (solanine formation is triggered by light and is mildly toxic)
source: Wikipedia — Solanine article: doses of 2–5 mg/kg of body weight cause toxic symptoms; 3–6 mg/kg can be fatal
notes: Light triggering solanine is correct. Describing solanine as 'mildly toxic' understates the risk — it causes gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms and can be fatal at higher doses. At GCSE level 'mildly toxic' is a common simplification but technically imprecise. Severity LOW as it is a known simplification in food education contexts.

title: Food Commodities & Their Place in the Diet
claim: A 200 ml glass of whole milk provides approximately 240 mg of calcium — about a quarter of the daily reference value for a teenager
source: Standard nutritional databases: whole milk ~120 mg calcium per 100 ml, so 200 ml ≈ 240 mg. UK NRV for calcium is 800 mg/day (adults); teenage recommendation is 1000 mg/day (11-18 years). 240 mg is approximately a quarter of 1000 mg.
notes: The 240 mg figure is correct. Calling it 'about a quarter' of teenage requirement is accurate (240/1000 = 24%).

title: Food Commodities & Their Place in the Diet
claim: Yoghurt is produced through the positive action of live Lactobacillus bacteria fermenting lactose
source: Wikipedia — Lactobacillus article confirms role in yoghurt fermentation; converts lactose to lactic acid
notes: Correct. Standard food science.

title: Food Commodities & Their Place in the Diet
claim: Margarine is produced by hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oils — early versions produced trans fats, which raised CVD risk; modern margarines use different methods to minimise trans fats
source: Wikipedia — Margarine and Hydrogenation articles confirm hydrogenation history and trans fat production/reduction
notes: Correct.

title: Effects on Wellbeing When Person-Centred Values Are NOT Applied
claim: Care Act 2014 (referenced implicitly via 'person-centred values' framework applicable to UK health and social care)
source: Wikipedia — Care Act 2014 article: real UK legislation, received royal assent 14 May 2014
notes: The lesson does not directly cite the Care Act 2014 by name but describes the person-centred values framework it underpins. Care Act 2014 is confirmed real legislation.

title: Effects on Wellbeing When Person-Centred Values Are NOT Applied
claim: The spec lists four intellectual effects: lack of progress or skills development, failure to achieve potential, loss of concentration, and lack of mental stimulation
source: OCR Cambridge National R032 / Level 2 Health & Social Care specification — standard PIES framework with these intellectual effects
notes: PIES framework with these intellectual effects is consistent with OCR specification content for Health and Social Care.

title: Effects on Wellbeing When Person-Centred Values Are NOT Applied
claim: The five physical effects the spec names are: pain if medication or treatment is not given; illness may get worse; malnutrition or illness due to lack of food for special dietary needs; dehydration due to lack of regular fluids; and injury
source: Standard OCR specification framework for R032 unit — these five physical effects are consistently listed in revision materials
notes: These are the standard five physical PIES effects per the OCR Cambridge National Health & Social Care specification.

title: How Parliament Works
claim: The House of Commons has 650 Members of Parliament (MPs), each representing a constituency
source: Wikipedia — House of Commons article: '650 members known as members of Parliament'
notes: Correct.

title: How Parliament Works
claim: bishops (26 senior Church of England bishops, known as Lords Spiritual)
source: Wikipedia — Lords Spiritual article: maximum of 26, currently 23 sitting
notes: The maximum of 26 is correct. The lesson is describing the constitutional maximum (26), which is accurate.

title: How Parliament Works
claim: hereditary peers (a small remaining group of 92, whose title passes down through their family following the House of Lords Act 1999)
source: Wikipedia — House of Lords Act 1999 article and House of Lords article: House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026 came into force 29 April 2026, removing all remaining hereditary peers
notes: This was accurate until 29 April 2026. The House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026 removed all 92 remaining hereditary peers. As of 29 April 2026 — one week before today — hereditary peers no longer sit in the Lords. The lesson presents this as current fact when the constitutional position has changed. Needs urgent update.

title: How Parliament Works
claim: The Lords scrutinise and can amend legislation passed by the Commons. They cannot permanently block Bills or legislation relating to finance (money Bills), but they can delay Bills by up to a year
source: Wikipedia — Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949: Lords can delay non-money bills by up to one year; money bills by one month
notes: Correct. The Parliament Act 1949 limits Lords' delay to one year for non-money bills.

title: How Parliament Works
claim: Prime Minister's Questions, held weekly when Parliament is sitting
source: Wikipedia — PMQs article: 'every Wednesday at noon when the House of Commons is sitting'
notes: Correct. PMQs is weekly (every Wednesday).

title: How Parliament Works
claim: Black Rod walks to the House of Commons to summon MPs; door shut in Black Rod's face — symbolising the Commons' independence from the Crown — before being opened after three knocks
source: Wikipedia — Black Rod article confirms door is slammed shut then Black Rod strikes three times with their staff before being admitted
notes: Correct.

title: Digital Democracy and Civic Participation
claim: On the UK Parliament petition website: 10,000 signatures = mandatory government response; 100,000 signatures = Parliament must consider a debate
source: Parliament petition website help page: thresholds confirmed at 10,000 and 100,000
notes: Correct.

title: Digital Democracy and Civic Participation
claim: Digital democracy describes how the internet and social media are reshaping the ways citizens engage with government
source: Wikipedia — Digital democracy article confirms definition and scope including e-petitions and social media
notes: Correct framing.
